repeticion.por_que:
The agent doesn't realize it already has the answer. It receives it, rereads the request and, since nothing in its instructions tells it when to stop, decides to look again. It keeps going round until it runs out of attempts.

It's the most common failure in agents that use tools, and it almost never raises an error: the agent ends up answering correctly. It just does the work several times.
repeticion.deteccion: Active rule: **{minimo} or more steps with the same `laplace.dedup_hash` within a single trace**. Ingestion computes the hash from the span type, its name, the model and the normalized input, so a change in key order or spacing doesn't count as a different input. Grouping is by trace first and then by hash: repeating within a run is a loop, showing up in different runs is normal use.
repeticion.arreglo.no_repetir.titulo: Tell the agent not to repeat itself
repeticion.arreglo.no_repetir.texto: Add one line to its instructions. It's a minute's work and it fixes most cases.
repeticion.arreglo.no_repetir.codigo:
# in your system prompt
If you have already called a tool and have the answer,
don't call it again. Answer with what you already know.
repeticion.arreglo.guardar.texto: If it asks for the same thing again within the same run, return what you already have instead of querying again.
repeticion.arreglo.tope.texto: Even after fixing the above, cap the rounds. That way, if it ever happens again, it costs you a few calls and not a cascade.

    ...  # and leave the loop once you have an answer

bucle.que_pasa: Within a single run, “{paso}” is called up to {veces} times. The inputs aren't identical (they differ in some number: an attempt counter, a page, a time), but across the {llamadas} calls in the window {salidas}. Many rounds and almost no new results is the measurable definition of going round without progress.
bucle.por_que:
The agent has an exit condition that is never met, or that depends on something it isn't looking at. Since a number changes on every round, it thinks it's doing something new: it asks again, gets the same answer and starts over until it runs out of attempts.

It's the hard sibling of exact repetition, which is why it's detected separately: a repetition shows up by comparing identical inputs, and here no two inputs are identical. What gives the loop away isn't the input, it's that the output doesn't change.
bucle.deteccion: Active rule: **{minimo} or more calls to the same step within a trace, with distinct inputs and at most {maximo} distinct outputs**. Ingestion computes `laplace.loop_hash` like `dedup_hash` but **ignoring the numbers** in the input, which is what makes a loop with a counter visible; the output hash doesn't ignore them, because there a changing number really is progress. Requiring distinct inputs is what stops this rule and the repetition rule from counting the same money twice.
bucle.arreglo.salida.texto: It's the first thing to look at: the loop exits at the attempt cap, not because it's done. Almost always, the check for the case where the answer is already final is missing.
bucle.arreglo.salida.codigo:
for attempt in range(MAX_ATTEMPTS):
    answer = {funcion}(...)
    if answer == previous:      # no progress: stop trying

    previous = answer

caro.lento.por_que:
A step that only has to choose between a few options doesn't need the most capable model, and the most capable one is usually also the slowest. As an agent grows, every step inherits the model it was first tried with.

The alternative comes from your own traffic, never from a list of models of ours.

cobertura.pasos.consecuencia: Calls that can't be told apart all fall into the same pile, so the rules can't compare one step with another and stay silent. A “nothing to fix” with this signal low means “we don't know”, not “it's fine”.
cobertura.pasos.arreglo: Decorate your agent's functions with @laplace.observe(type="agent") or wrap them in laplace.span(...): that way Laplace knows where the model is called from. If you have payloads turned off (capture_content=False), it can't use the instructions either.
cobertura.tarifa.label: Calls with a known price
cobertura.tarifa.consecuencia: What has no price doesn't cost zero: it costs “we don't know”. Until this signal is at 100%, the spend below is a floor, and so is the saving.
cobertura.tarifa.arreglo: If it's a provider's model, write its price in a JSON of your own ({{"models": {{"model-name": {{"input": 1.0, "output": 4.0}}}}}}, in dollars per million tokens, from its official page) and start Laplace with LAPLACE_PRICES_EXTRA pointing to that file. If it runs on your machine (Ollama, LM Studio), there's no price to add: nobody charges you. Then this signal stays at zero on purpose, money can't be calculated, and the rules talk to you about tokens and time, which are measured.
cobertura.tokens.label: Calls with provider-reported tokens
cobertura.tokens.consecuencia: The tokens we count ourselves are an approximation, and so is the cost derived from them. A figure from the bill isn't the same as one from dividing characters by four. Note: a failed call doesn't bring tokens either, and also lowers this signal: there's nothing to estimate there, there simply was no answer.
cobertura.tokens.arreglo: First check whether they're failed calls (a provider outage counts them all here). If not, ask for the count when streaming: in OpenAI, stream_options={{"include_usage": True}}.

cobertura.prompts.consecuencia: Without a version in the trace, there's no telling which version of a prompt cost what or which was more accurate: the Prompts tab makes do with what it can infer from the instructions.
cobertura.prompts.arreglo: Move the prompt into Laplace and fetch it with laplace.get_prompt("name"). It's optional: the rest of the product works the same without it.

Move that data into variables and Laplace will be able to tell you which version costs what.
prompts.simultaneas: These instructions run together in the same run: they're different calls from the same place in your code, not versions of a prompt.

prompt_caro.titulo: v{b} of “{prompt}” costs {pct} more per run than v{a}
prompt_caro.lead: Going back to v{a} recovers it, if it's just as accurate.
prompt_caro.resumen: Since “{prompt}” went from v{a} to v{b}, every run that uses it costs {coste_b} instead of {coste_a}. Over {trazas} runs with v{b}, that's {extra} extra.
prompt_caro.que_pasa: The calls made with v{a} of “{prompt}” cost {coste_a} per run ({trazas_a} runs); those made with v{b}, the one running now, {coste_b} ({trazas_b} runs). The rest of the agent doesn't count here: this is the cost of the calls that use this prompt.
prompt_caro.por_que:
A prompt change is decided by what it answers, and what it costs shows up later, on the bill. Longer instructions are paid on every call, and ones that ask for more detail make every answer longer.

v{b} may be worth what it costs: if it's more accurate, the difference is the price of that improvement. That's why this doesn't claim it's waste, only how much the change costs.
prompt_caro.deteccion: Active rule: **the version of a managed prompt running now costs more than {umbral} more per run than the previous one**, with at least {minimo} runs on each and all of their calls priced. Evaluation runs are left out, as in the other rules. If other problems already claim part of the cost of the new version's calls, the difference is only counted on what's left: fixes compound, and the same money isn't counted twice.
prompt_caro.consulta: Cost and runs per (prompt_name, prompt_version), without evaluation runs: the same read as the Prompts tab (prompt_usage), with each version's step identities.
prompt_caro.arreglo.comparar.titulo: Compare how accurate each version is
prompt_caro.arreglo.comparar.texto: In Prompts, the card for “{prompt}” puts v{a} and v{b} side by side, with how accurate each one is. If there aren't enough annotations, test both on the same real calls (below): if v{b} is more accurate, it may be worth it.
prompt_caro.arreglo.volver.texto: If they're equally accurate, put v{a} in production from Prompts. It's one click and doesn't touch the code: the SDK picks it up in under a minute.
prompt_caro.arreglo.recortar.titulo: Or keep what improved and drop what makes it expensive
prompt_caro.arreglo.recortar.texto: The diff on the card for “{prompt}” shows what changed from v{a} to v{b}. If what makes it expensive is added examples or context, caching or trimming them keeps the improvement for less.
prompt_caro.ahorro: With v{a}: {coste_a} per run. With v{b}: {coste_b}. The difference over the {trazas} runs of v{b} is {bruto}. Other problems on those same calls already claim {reclamado} of the {total} they cost, and fixing them also makes the difference cheaper: the remaining {parte} is counted, {neto} in {ventana}.{proyeccion}
prompt_caro.nota: The difference is measured on real calls from both versions. What we don't know is whether the new one is more accurate: Prompts' annotations or a run in the Test tab will tell you.

compartida.titulo: {pasos} steps send the same {tokens}-token prefix without sharing the cache
compartida.resumen: Steps {pasos} start with the same instructions, at least {tokens} tokens, and are called {llamadas} times across {trazas} runs. Within each run, the provider's cache could serve that prefix to all of them but the first.{precio}
compartida.precio: Sharing it would save {ahorro} in this window.
compartida.lead: Several steps with the same system prompt, each paying for it in full.
compartida.que_pasa: Steps {pasos} are called from different places in the code, but they start with the same instructions: the shortest call of all of them already carries {tokens} tokens. In the window they were called {llamadas} times across {trazas} runs, so each run sends that prefix several times.
compartida.por_que: Providers' prompt caches know nothing about steps: they reuse any identical prefix they have seen recently. If two steps send exactly the same beginning, the second one can read it from cache at a fraction of the price. Step by step it doesn't show, because each one is called only once per run.
compartida.deteccion: Active rule: **two or more `llm` steps with the same instructions-and-tools fingerprint (`prefix_hash`) and the same model, with at least {llamadas} calls between them and a minimum input above {minimo} tokens**. It counts the calls that would hit a warm cache within each run, minus those the per-step fixed-context rule already counts.
compartida.arreglo.igual.texto: The cache only reuses an exactly equal beginning: same instructions, same tools, in the same order. Put what is shared first and what changes from step to step after it.
compartida.arreglo.marca.titulo: Mark the end of the shared part
compartida.arreglo.marca.texto: On Anthropic, put the `cache_control` at the end of what the steps share, not at the end of each one's own part. OpenAI caches prefixes over 1,024 tokens on its own, if they are identical.
compartida.ahorro: {tokens} fixed tokens × ({llamadas} calls − {trazas} runs) = {lecturas} tokens that would hit a warm cache, of which the per-step fixed context already counts {ya}; of the rest, {parte} is not served from cache today and would go from {entrada}/1M to {cacheada}/1M. Minus the first write of each run, {escritura}. Net: {neto} in {ventana}.{proyeccion}
compartida.nota: This is a conservative estimate: the shared prefix is at most the shortest call of all the steps, and the cache is assumed not to survive from one run to the next.
